notes.content: Topics: Heat and Temperature | Thermal Expansion | Quantity of Heat | Rate of Heat Flow | Ideal Gas
Before 19th century: **Caloric Theory** — heat believed to be a fine, weightless fluid ('caloric') hiding in the pores of a substance, flowing like a liquid/gas.
key_points: Caloric theory: object contains fixed amount of caloric; adding caloric → temperature ↑; removing → temperature ↓
Caloric was assumed odorless, tasteless, invisible — never actually detected
FLAW: could not explain **heat generated by friction** (rubbing two metals in water can boil it — limitless heat generation contradicts a 'fixed amount' fluid)
**Davy and Joule** established heat as a *form of energy*, arising from mechanical motion of particles
Modern concept: Internal energy = total energy (kinetic + vibrational + rotational) of all molecules of a body; when this flows between bodies due to temperature difference, it is called heat
notes.quote: "Order is manifestly maintained in the universe... governed by the sovereign will of God." — James Prescott Joule

notes.section: 9.2 Heat: Transfer of Energy due to Temperature Difference
notes.definition: **Heat** is the form of energy which flows from one body to another due to temperature difference.
notes.important_note: A body does NOT contain heat — heat is not a property of a body (analogous to how work is not 'contained' in a body, only done on/by it). Heat only exists as energy *in transit*.
notes.example: Hot iron ball dropped in water → temperature of water increases, temperature of ball decreases until both reach same temperature. The 'something' transferred = heat.

notes.derivation_from_notebook: Heat = energy = work done = F × d = (m·a)·d = [M][LT^-2][L] = [M L^2 T^-2]

notes.content: We commonly say a body 'contains heat' — this is INCORRECT. Just as it's wrong to say work is 'in' a body, it's wrong to say heat is 'in' a body. Heat exists only when there is FLOW due to temperature difference; once flow stops, the word 'heat' cannot be used — only 'internal energy' can.
notes.analogy: Like a bus passenger vs. a pedestrian — same person, but the label depends on the *condition* (whether energy is flowing or not).

notes.definition: **Temperature** is the thermal condition that determines the direction of flow of heat from one body to another; i.e., the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
key_facts: Hot/cold are RELATIVE terms (like motion/rest, left/right)

Classic demo: hand from hot water + hand from cold water, both placed in tepid water → tepid water feels cool to the 'hot-water hand' and warm to the 'cold-water hand' — same temperature, different sensation
Heat flows spontaneously from HIGH temperature → LOW temperature body
No upper limit of temperature; lower limit = **0 Kelvin** (temperature cannot go below 0 K)

content: 1757: **Joseph Black** discovered latent heat, first to distinguish temperature from heat.

A brick at 20°C broken into unequal pieces → BOTH pieces remain at 20°C (temperature is independent of size), but the LARGER piece has MORE internal energy (temperature is an *intensive* quantity, unlike heat/internal energy which is *extensive*).

notes.section: 9.4 Molecular Concept: Thermal Energy, Heat Energy, Temperature
notes.content: Molecules of matter are in constant motion (translational, rotational, vibrational) → kinetic energy. Intermolecular forces → potential energy.
definitions: **Thermal energy (internal energy)** = sum of kinetic + potential energies of all molecules of a body
**Temperature** = the effect/measure of thermal energy in a body — higher thermal energy → higher temperature
**Heat energy** = thermal energy *transferred* from one body to another due to temperature difference — i.e., 'heat is thermal energy in transit'

notes.section: 9.5 Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
notes.definition: **Thermal equilibrium**: a number of bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if they have the same temperature, so there is NO NET exchange of heat between them.
notes.zeroth_law_statement: If two systems (A and B) are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system (C), then A and B are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.
notes.history: Propounded by **R. H. Fowler**. Came to light only in **1930** — much later than the 1st and 2nd laws — yet is fundamental to both, hence placed 'before' them and called the **Zeroth Law**.
significance: (i) It defines temperature of a body
(ii) Establishes temperature as a valid, fundamental concept underlying 1st & 2nd laws
(iii) Common misconception: 'no flow of heat' in thermal equilibrium is WRONG — heat always flows both ways between bodies even at equilibrium, but the NET flow is zero
notes.figure_note: Fig 9.2: A—B directly linked; A—C and B—C linked via dashed lines representing separate equilibrium, concluding A≡B

notes.section: 9.6 Cause and Direction of Heat Flow
notes.content: Heat flows from high-temperature to low-temperature region because molecules at higher temperature have more thermal energy; during collisions, energy transfers from high-thermal-energy molecules to low-thermal-energy ones until equilibrium — at which point no net energy transfer occurs (no force acts through a distance, so no work is done).
notes.key_definition: **Heat is the spontaneous transfer of thermal energy from higher to lower temperature to attain thermal equilibrium.** Cause of heat flow = temperature difference (NOT internal energy difference).
notes.important_example: 50 kg of water at 30°C in contact with 200 g of water at 25°C → heat flows from 30°C water to 25°C water, even though the 25°C water (being 50 kg... wait, correction: the LARGER mass) has far more total internal energy. Direction depends on TEMPERATURE, not total internal energy.

notes.definition: **Thermometry** = study of measurement of temperature of a body. Basic principle: two bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.
notes.history: Earliest thermometer constructed by **Galileo (1593)**; **Newton** suggested the necessity of fixed points.
notes.working_principle: Thermal equilibrium is the working principle of a mercury thermometer — heat transfers between substance and thermometer until both reach the SAME temperature (equilibrium); the thermometer reading = its own temperature = the substance's temperature.

notes.principle: Uses expansion/contraction of mercury with temperature change; volume of mercury ∝ temperature.
advantages: Mercury expands more than six times uniformly (linear expansion) over usable range
Since it is a liquid metal, it therefore conducts heat well and reaches thermometer's own temperature quickly, giving correct readings
Does not wet glass and can easily be found in pure form
Opaque and shiny — easy to take reading
Not very sensitive — doesn't take much heat from body being measured, so reading stays accurate
Practically non-volatile, so not affected much by its vapour pressure
disadvantages: Cannot measure temperature below -39°C (freezing point of mercury)
Not suitable in very cold regions

clinical_thermometer.range: 94°F to 108°F (marked on the special clinical thermometer used for humans)
clinical_thermometer.feature: Has a constriction (kink) near the bulb that prevents mercury from flowing back automatically — must be 'jerked' to reset reading below the bulb's contracted thread

sensitivity_factors: Fineness of the capillary bore (thinner bore = more sensitive, more rise for small temp change)
Bulb size (bigger bulb = more liquid = more expansion = more sensitive)
Thermal conductivity of the bulb material (thin conducting bulb wall = faster response = more sensitive)
Nature/expansivity of the thermometric liquid used

notes.range: Used to measure temperatures BELOW -39°C (mercury's freezing point) — good for very cold regions
advantages: Alcohol expands more than mercury (about six times) for same temperature rise — MORE SENSITIVE
Freezing point (-130°C) is much lower than mercury (-39°C), so suitable for very cold climates
disadvantages: Cannot measure above 78°C (its own boiling point)
It wets the wall of the glass tube
Not conducting → slow to reach equilibrium, less uniform expansion

notes.content: Created by identifying two easily-reproducible fixed temperatures (usually freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure), then dividing the interval into equal divisions.

scales.name: Celsius (Centigrade) Scale
scales.lower_fixed_point: 0°C (ice point / melting point of pure ice)
scales.upper_fixed_point: 100°C (steam point / boiling point of water at 760 mm Hg)

scales.name: Kelvin (Absolute) Scale
scales.divisions: 100 equal parts, same size as Celsius degree
scales.special_note: Absolute zero = 0 K = -273.15°C = lowest possible temperature = point where properties of ideal gas (theoretically) vanish; it is INDEPENDENT of properties of thermometers.
scales.capitalization_rule: CAUTION: On Kelvin scale, measurement of temperature is conventionally written WITHOUT the degree symbol (°) — write 1 K, NOT 1°K. Kelvin (unit) is NOT capitalized when written out, but capital 'K' IS used as abbreviation.

scales.name: Reaumur Scale
scales.introduced_by: Reaumur (French philosopher), 1730 A.D., used mainly in Russia

scales.name: Rankine Scale
scales.divisions: 180 equal parts (each division = same size as Fahrenheit degree)

notes.content: **Absolute zero** = the lowest possible temperature theoretically attainable in the universe = -273.15°C = 0 K. It is defined as an ABSOLUTE property, independent of any thermometric substance — unlike ice/steam points which depend on properties of water.
notes.recorded_lab_minimum: 1.0 × 10^-10 K (recorded in lab, at Boomerang Nebula ~1 K, on Earth's surface at Vostok, Antarctica: 183 K ≈ -89°C)

notes.section: Difference between Degree Centigrade (C°) and Centigrade Degree (°C)
notes.content: **°C** denotes an actual TEMPERATURE (a point on the scale). **C°** denotes a temperature INTERVAL or DIFFERENCE (a change in temperature).
notes.example: A change in temperature of 25°C = a temperature interval of 25 C° = a temperature change of 45 F°.
notes.formula: ΔC = (5/9) × ΔF  → i.e. a difference in centigrade scale = (5/9) × difference in Fahrenheit scale

notes.section: Master Formula — Relation between Temperature Scales
notes.general_relation: (C - Lower fixed pt.) / (Upper fixed pt. − Lower fixed pt.) is SAME for every scale
notes.note: θ1 = Lower fixed point of faulty thermometer, θ2 = Upper fixed point of faulty thermometer, n = number of divisions between them; use (C-0)/100 = (θ-θ1)/n for faulty thermometer problems

notes.content: A faulty thermometer's fixed points are NOT correctly marked at 0° and 100° (unlike a correct Celsius thermometer). Its scale must be related back to the true Celsius scale using ratio of intervals.
notes.formula: (C - 0)/(100 - 0) = (Faulty reading - Lower fixed pt.)/(Upper fixed pt. - Lower fixed pt.)

notes.section: 9.9 Do Thermometers Agree at Any Temperature? (Stop to Think 9.5)
notes.question: Do you consider a temperature value at which Celsius and Kelvin thermometers agree?
notes.answer: No — since K = C + 273.15, there is NO temperature at which Celsius and Kelvin readings are numerically equal.

notes.question: Absolute zero = -273.15°C. Find value on Fahrenheit scale.

parts.given: 31.1°C (highest annual avg temp in USA) → Fahrenheit

notes.section: Worked Example 2 — Faulty Thermometer (Melting/Boiling Point of Water)
notes.question: A faulty thermometer has fixed points marked as 5° and 95°. It reads 59° for melting point of ice and boiling point at 60°C actual. Find the actual reading and number of divisions.
notes.method: Use (C-0)/n = (θ-θ1)/n with lower fixed point θ1 = -10°C found via ratio; solved n = 140, θ1 = -10°C giving the faulty scale spans -10°C to 130°C actual equivalent
notes.note: See full working in textbook — establishes θ2 = 130°C for the boiling point equivalent.

notes.section: Worked Example 3 — Correcting a Faulty Thermometer Body Temperature
notes.question: Faulty thermometer: melting point of ice = 5°, boiling point of water = 95°. Body temperature measured = 59° on faulty scale. Find correct Celsius temperature.
notes.formula_used: (C-0)/(100-0) = (Faulty reading - Lower fixed pt)/(Upper fixed pt - Lower fixed pt) = (59-5)/(95-5) = 54/90

notes.question: Faulty thermometer marked -2° and 98° at correct 20° and 98°(?) — normal body temp shown as x°C? [see Ans]

notes.section: Stop to Think 9.4 — Reaumur & Rankine Scale Answer
notes.question: A thermometer reads 20° on Celsius and correct temperature reads 80°R (Reaumur). What is Rankine value etc.? Convert to °C.
notes.note: Given: θ1=98°, θ2=-2°, U1=0°C, U2=100°C, and relation used: (θ1-L1)/(U1-L1) = (θ2-L2)/(U2-L2). Normal human body temp calculation gave x = 22°C.

notes.question: If your doctor tells you that your temperature is 310 K, should you worry? (310 K equivalent to 98.6°F, human body normal temp)
notes.answer: No need to worry — 310 K = 36.85°C ≈ 98.6°F, which is a NORMAL human body temperature.

notes.section: Numerical Example 6-8 — Sensitivity, Bore Size, Response
content: Why is the triple point of water chosen as a standard fixed point in modern thermometry? → It's the unique point where solid, liquid, and vapour phases of water coexist in equilibrium; it is highly reproducible unlike melting/boiling points which depend on pressure/impurities.

Why should a thermometer bulb have a small heat capacity? → So it absorbs less heat from the body being measured, and its own temperature changes quickly to match the object being measured, giving a fast and accurate reading without altering the object's temperature.

Why is bore of capillary tube of a thermometer chosen to be uniform? → So the graduations/scale divisions are equal throughout, since mercury is more sensitive & expansive than a gas thread; ensures reading correctness.

content.definition: The temperature at which pure ice melts at normal atmospheric pressure.
The temperature at which pure water boils at normal atmospheric pressure.

notes.content: Two bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if there is no flow of heat between them when placed in contact. If heat flows from body A to body B, then the temperature of A is GREATER than B (heat flows from hotter to colder body, from higher to lower temperature).
notes.three_body_case: Consider bodies A, B and C. If A & C are in thermal equilibrium, and B & C are also in thermal equilibrium, then A & B must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. → This is Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics.

notes.derivation: Temperature is a fundamental quantity in SI units.

answers.9.2: The thermometer measures ITS OWN temperature, which — after reaching thermal equilibrium with the body — becomes equal to the body's temperature too.

notes.content: To measure LOW temperature, liquid thermometers work up to about -1000°C to 1000°C using resistance thermometers; for VERY HIGH temperature (up to 3000°C and beyond), a device called **Pyrometer** is used.
notes.definition: **Pyrometry** = the measurement of very high temperatures (e.g. of sun, stars, blast furnace) using a Pyrometer, since ordinary thermometers cannot be used at such extreme temperatures.
notes.kelvin_reference: The Kelvin scale is preferred and standard for ALL accurate scientific temperature measurements, referred to in preference to all other thermometers.
